passage: Monday: Manoj, almost two, tumbles off the low step and wails. Dadi is nearest; she scoops him up, and he quiets against her shoulder. Wednesday: Chachi is chopping onions when Manoj bumps his head on the table leg. He toddles straight to her knee, and she rubs the spot. Saturday: Manoj trips in the courtyard. His cousin Ayesha, nine, pulls him onto her lap and sings. He stops crying and pats her cheek, grinning.

qa.q: Who comforted Manoj on Saturday when he tripped in the courtyard?
qa.a: His cousin Ayesha pulled him onto her lap and sang.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling on Wednesday when he toddled to Chachi's knee, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt hurt and a little frightened after bumping his head, but safe with Chachi; he went to her on his own and calmed while she rubbed the spot.

qa.q: What could the family keep doing so Manoj stays secure with everyone at home?
qa.a: Keep answering his cries quickly, whoever is closest, with a lap, a song or a gentle rub, so every familiar face stays a safe place.

qa.q: What is it like for Ayesha when Manoj stops crying and pats her cheek?
qa.a: Ayesha probably feels proud and trusted, because her small cousin chose her lap and settled with her song.

grounding: Shows a toddler in a joint household being soothed by whichever relative is nearest, so his sense of safety spreads across a grandmother, an aunt and a cousin.

passage: In a third-floor flat in Chennai, eighteen-month-old Keerthana lives with Paati, Thatha, her parents, Chithi Ritu and two cousins. When the pressure cooker whistles, she howls; Thatha, on the sofa with his paper, holds out his arms and she climbs in. Later Amma steps out for vegetables. Keerthana frowns at the door until Ritu hands her a steel cup to bang, and she laughs. By evening she is asleep on Paati's lap in the middle of all the chatter.

qa.q: What did Ritu give Keerthana after Amma stepped out?
qa.a: Ritu handed her a steel cup to bang.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when the pressure cooker whistled, and how did she settle?
qa.a: She was startled and scared by the loud whistle, and felt safe again once she climbed into Thatha's arms.

qa.q: What helps a toddler like Keerthana cope when one caregiver leaves the room?
qa.a: Another familiar person stepping in quickly with play or comfort, as Ritu did, so the gap never feels empty.

qa.q: How might Amma feel if she came back and saw Keerthana laughing with Ritu?
qa.a: Amma may feel relieved and a little wistful, knowing her daughter is happy with the other familiar faces at home.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler in a large city household whose crying is soothed by whoever is closest, so her attachment spreads across grandparents, parents and an aunt.

passage:
'Leela, Mama's just going to get the clothes off the line.'
'Mama! Mama!'
'Two minutes, sweetheart. Papa's right here.'
'Noooo! Mama!'
'Look, Leela, blocks!'
Papa calls through the balcony door, 'Ayesha, she's standing at the door, crying.'
'Coming!' Ayesha hurries in, and two-year-old Leela runs to her Mama and hiccups into her kurta.
'See? Back already.'
Later the three of them eat quietly, Leela's hand on Mama's sleeve.

qa.q: What was Mama going to do when she left the room?
qa.a: She was going to get the clothes off the line.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when Mama went to the balcony, and what shows it?
qa.a: Leela felt upset and afraid that Mama was gone; she kept calling 'Mama!', refused the blocks and stood crying at the door.

qa.q: What could the parents try so short separations feel easier for Leela?
qa.a: Say a warm goodbye, tell her when Mama will be back, and sometimes let her come along or watch, so she learns Mama always returns.

qa.q: What is it like for Papa when Leela refuses his blocks and cries for Mama?
qa.a: Papa may feel a bit helpless or left out, because his comfort is not enough in that moment even though he is right there.

grounding: Shows a toddler in a small family who is closely bonded to one caregiver and becomes sharply distressed when that caregiver leaves the room.

passage:

Aadhya, two, lives with just her parents; her days are usually quiet. When her father waved and left, she cried hard and held the door handle a long time, deaf to the other children. I sat near her without pulling her away and said, 'You miss Papa.' She let me read her the duck book. At pickup she ran to him and would not let go. I have asked him to stay five minutes tomorrow.

qa.a: The duck book.

qa.q: How was Aadhya feeling when her father left, and what shows it?

qa.q: How might Aadhya's father feel when she runs to him and will not let go at pickup?
qa.a: He may feel loved and also a little worried, seeing how strongly she depends on him and her mother.

passage:
At the kindergarten lunch table, five-year-old Jatin opens his tiffin and, without a word, tears his paratha in half for his cousin Siddharth, who forgot his box. Ten minutes later they are tugging the same green crayon.
'Mine!'
'I had it first!'
It snaps, both howl, and Rekha Ma'am kneels between them. Before she can speak, Jatin hands over the longer piece, Siddharth gives him a sticker, and they go back to colouring one shared page. A classmate, hugging her own box, asks, 'Don't you want your own paper?' Jatin just looks puzzled.

qa.q: What did Jatin share with Siddharth at lunch?
qa.a: Half of his paratha.

qa.q: Why did Jatin look puzzled when the classmate asked about his own paper, and what was he feeling?
qa.a: He felt comfortable and happy sharing; with his cousin, one page for two seems normal, so wanting separate paper made no sense to him.

qa.q: What could Rekha Ma'am learn from how the boys made up?
qa.a: She could let them try to fix small quarrels themselves first and notice the quick repair, while staying close in case it does not settle.

qa.q: How might the classmate with her own box see the cousins' sharing?
qa.a: She may find it surprising or odd, since she keeps her own things, and might even wish for such an easy partner.

grounding: Shows a young child raised among cousins who shares food and things without being told, fights and makes up fast, and has no need yet for his own space.

passage:
From my balcony next door I watch Kavitha, five, and her four cousins sleep in one heap on a single mattress on their terrace on summer nights. Yesterday a mango came up. Kavitha bit it and passed it along without anyone asking; the smallest got the seed to suck. Later I heard a squabble over who got the spot by the wall, tears and a shove, and five minutes after, all of them giggling under one sheet. My daughter asked me why Kavitha doesn't have her own room. I didn't know. Kavitha never seems to want one.
Sangeeta

qa.q: Where do Kavitha and her cousins sleep on summer nights?
qa.a: On a single mattress on their terrace.

qa.q: What does Kavitha passing the mango along suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels happy and at ease sharing, as if belonging with her cousins is simply normal, though Sangeeta can only guess from outside.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta tell the daughter who asked about Kavitha's room?
qa.a: That families live in different ways: Kavitha shares a lot and seems to enjoy it, and having your own room is fine too.

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta's daughter find Kavitha's life puzzling?
qa.a: The daughter probably has a separate room and things, so sharing a bed and a mango with many cousins looks strange.

grounding: Illustrates a young child among cousins who shares bed and food unasked, fights and makes up quickly, and does not seem to miss privacy, as seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Sunday: At the family lunch, Bua announces that cousin Mohit got 96 in maths. Papa turns to Amandeep. 'And you? 81? See, Mohit studies.' Amandeep smiles, pushes rice around the plate, and leaves half.
Wednesday: After school, Amandeep sits at the desk doing extra sums nobody set, lips pressed tight. When Mummy peeks in, Amandeep says, 'I'll beat Mohit next time,' but slams the book when one sum goes wrong.
Saturday: Mohit phones to ask for help with a drawing project. Amandeep helps, then asks Mummy quietly, 'Would you love me more if I was Mohit?' Mummy sits down and takes Amandeep's hand. 'Never. Marks are not you.'

qa.q: What did Mohit score in maths?
qa.a: Mohit got 96 in maths.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when Papa compared the marks at lunch?
qa.a: Amandeep felt hurt and embarrassed, hiding it behind a smile and leaving half the rice.

qa.q: What could Papa do differently when marks come up at family lunches?
qa.a: Talk about Amandeep's own effort and progress in private, instead of holding up Mohit as the standard in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Mohit be affected by always being held up as the example?
qa.a: Mohit might feel awkward or pressured to keep scoring high, and the comparisons could make things tense between the cousins.

grounding: Shows a child whose score is compared with a cousin's and who reacts with both extra effort and a quiet hurt about not being enough.

passage: Suraj, you think your Nani never had a bad report card? Sit. When I was nine, in our big house in Jabalpur, my cousin Kamla came first every year. Every evening Tauji would say, 'Look at Kamla, Minakshi, and look at you.' So I started waking at five to study, and yes, my sums got better. But I also stopped singing, because Kamla sang better too. One day Masi found me crying behind the water tank. No lecture. Masi only asked, 'Kamla is Kamla. What do you like?' I said, 'Drawing.' The next week Masi bought me a tin of colours. I still have that tin.

qa.q: What did Masi buy for young Minakshi?
qa.a: Masi bought a tin of colours.

qa.q: How did young Minakshi feel about being compared to Kamla every evening?
qa.a: She felt hurt and never good enough; she pushed herself to study at five in the morning, but stopped singing and ended up crying behind the water tank.

qa.q: Which turning point in the story helped young Minakshi most, and why?
qa.a: Masi asking what she liked instead of lecturing, because it gave her something of her own that was not a contest with Kamla.

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt hearing Tauji hold up the marks every evening?
qa.a: Kamla may have felt proud but also uneasy, and the constant comparison could have put distance between the two cousins.

grounding: Illustrates a child compared with a higher-scoring cousin who feels both driven to work harder and a quiet hurt of never being enough.

passage:
Monday: After the evening prayer, Nani notices nine-year-old Hafsa on the next mat, murmuring the same words half a beat behind, copying even the way Nani lowers her forehead. Nani says nothing, but folds her mat very slowly.
Thursday: Hafsa spills a glass of milk and says, 'Sabr, sabr,' exactly in Nani's tone. Nani laughs out loud.
Sunday: Hafsa's friend Lakshmi visits, and Hafsa retells Nani's story of the thirsty crow and the pot, word for word, even the pause before the ending. Lakshmi begs for another. That night Nani tells Hafsa's Ammi, 'They listen, you know. All of it stays.'

qa.q: Which story did Hafsa retell to Lakshmi?
qa.a: Nani's story of the thirsty crow and the pot.

qa.q: What was Nani feeling when she said, 'They listen, you know. All of it stays'?
qa.a: Nani felt moved and proud, sensing that her prayers, sayings and stories really matter in Hafsa's life.

qa.q: What could Hafsa's Ammi do to keep this learning going?
qa.a: Make time for Hafsa to sit with Nani for prayers and stories, and perhaps ask Nani to share a new saying now and then.

qa.q: How does Hafsa seem to see Nani's words and stories?
qa.a: Hafsa seems to treasure them, repeating Nani's sayings in the same tone and proudly passing the story on to Lakshmi.

grounding: Shows a grandmother noticing a grandchild copy her prayers, sayings and stories through daily contact, and feeling that her role has meaning.

passage: Gurleen, you asked how your baby will ever learn Punjabi here, with both grandmothers so far away. Let your Aparna Dida tell you something. When my son's family lived with me in Kolkata, I said my evening prayers aloud and told stories while shelling peas. I thought nobody listened. Then one afternoon I heard my grandson Tuhin, nine, telling his little sister, 'Slowly, slowly, the river fills the sea,' in my exact sing-song, finger raised like mine. Another day he corrected his father's Bangla. I sat on the steps and cried a little, happy. Nobody had given me that job. It came from simply being there every day.

qa.q: What saying did Tuhin tell his little sister?
qa.a: 'Slowly, slowly, the river fills the sea.'

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she sat on the steps and cried a little?
qa.a: Aparna felt happy and moved, realising her prayers, stories and sayings had been passing to Tuhin just through everyday life.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed how Aparna saw the daily prayers and stories, and why?
qa.a: Hearing Tuhin repeat her saying in her exact sing-song; it showed that simply being present every day was already teaching him.

qa.q: How might Tuhin have seen Aparna's everyday stories at the time?
qa.a: To Tuhin they were probably just part of home, so natural that he copied them, gesture and all, without thinking of them as lessons.

grounding: Illustrates a grandmother who notices a grandchild copying her sayings, prayers and stories through daily contact and feels her role has meaning.

passage:
At the back table of the school library, Hemant has spread out his notes but isn't reading.
'You okay?' Kunal whispers.
'Only place I can think,' Hemant mutters. 'Eleven people in four rooms at home. Last night I called Sir about the project and Chachi, Dadi and my cousin all heard every word. Then Dadi asked what I was hiding.'
'So what did you do?'
'Slammed the door. It doesn't even lock. Papa shouted. I felt like the worst person.'
Kunal taps his pen. 'Maybe just ask for one hour after dinner. Door closed.'
'Won't that sound selfish?'
'Less selfish than slamming it.'
Hemant half-laughs.

qa.q: How many people live in Hemant's home?
qa.a: Eleven people in four rooms.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he slammed the door?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and exposed after relatives overheard his call and asked what he was hiding, and afterwards guilty, 'like the worst person'.

qa.q: What could Hemant say at home instead of slamming the door?
qa.a: Calmly ask for a set time, like one hour after dinner with the door closed, and explain it is for calls and study, not secrets.

qa.q: How might Dadi see Hemant's closed door and private call?
qa.a: Dadi may read it as secrecy or distance, since in a close household a hidden call can feel like being shut out.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a crowded joint home who wants a private call and a closed door, but whose need for space bursts out as a slammed door because asking feels selfish.

passage:
Dear Dolma,
You're lucky you have a hostel room, even if you share it with one person. Here, Nani sleeps in my room since her knee got worse, Mummy's cousin is staying 'for a few weeks', and the only door that locks is the bathroom. Yesterday I took the phone into the bathroom to talk to you and Mausi knocked three times. I came out and snapped at everyone, then sulked through dinner.
I know they love me. I love them. That's exactly why I can't say 'Please leave me alone.' It sounds so ungrateful.
How do you ask for space without hurting anyone?
Darshan

qa.q: Which is the only door that locks in Darshan's home?
qa.a: The bathroom door.

qa.q: What is Darshan feeling while asking Dolma for advice?
qa.a: Darshan feels torn: frustrated at having no private space, yet guilty, because asking to be left alone seems ungrateful to a loving family.

qa.q: What could Darshan try instead of sulking through dinner?
qa.a: Pick a calm moment and ask for something small and specific, like a quiet half-hour in the room each evening, while showing care for the family.

qa.q: How might Mausi feel after knocking and then facing Darshan's snapping?
qa.a: Mausi might feel hurt or confused, since the knocks were probably ordinary and not meant to intrude.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a crowded joint home who wants a private phone call, but because asking for space feels selfish, it comes out as snapping and sulking.

passage:
Hi Zainab,
It's 4:40 and the flat is so quiet I can hear the fridge. Mumma's shift ends at eight, Papa's at nine. I can eat what I want, watch what I want, and nobody asks about homework. Sounds great, right? Nobody here even knows I got the part in the school play yet. Maybe I'll tell them at dinner, if they aren't too tired.
Write back soon, okay? 🙂
Kashish

qa.q: What time does Mumma's shift end?
qa.a: Mumma's shift ends at eight.

qa.q: What is Kashish feeling while writing about the quiet flat?
qa.a: Kashish feels lonely, even though the freedom is real; the videos are mostly there to fill the silence.

qa.q: What small step could help Kashish feel less alone after school?
qa.a: Tell Mumma and Papa about the play and the quiet afternoons, and set up regular calls with Zainab or join an after-school activity.

qa.q: How might Kashish's parents feel if they learned about the lonely afternoons?
qa.a: They would likely feel sad and a little guilty, and might look for ways to connect, like a quick call from work or a shared dinner ritual.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager with two working parents who enjoys freedom after school but feels lonely without relatives around, and lets screens fill the silence.

passage: 'You want to know why I'm always online at three in the afternoon, Shreya? Okay. Mom's a nurse, nights mostly, so she's asleep when I get home. Dad works on a ship, gone for months. So it's me, a sleeping mom and a closed door. Nobody shouting, nobody fighting over the TV. My cousins in Nagpur live six to a flat, and I used to feel sorry for them. Now I kind of envy the noise. I put on a game just so there are voices talking. Some days I play till dinner without noticing the time. Honestly, the best part of my day is this walk with you.' Madhav kicks a pebble and doesn't look up.

qa.a: Mom's a nurse, working nights mostly.

qa.q: What does Madhav feel about the quiet afternoons at home?
qa.a: Madhav feels lonely; the freedom is real, but the silence hurts enough that Madhav envies the cousins' noise and plays games just to hear voices.

qa.a: Plan some regular company, like walks with Shreya, a club or calls with the cousins, and tell Mom how the afternoons feel.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel hearing that the walk is the best part of Madhav's day?
qa.a: Shreya might feel touched and a bit concerned, and may want to spend more time together after school.

passage:
By the time Pradeep came back from the bus stand, the whole verandah had decided. Bade Papa said engineering in the district town. Chachi said a government job was safer. Phupha had already asked someone about coaching fees. Pradeep stood holding the veterinary diploma form his friend Asif had helped him fill at the cyber cafe. His chest tightened, but he sat down.
'Thank you for thinking so much about me,' he said. 'Tell me your worries.'
He listened to all of them, and even nodded at Chachi's point about fees. Then he said, 'I'll think about everything. But I love the animals on our farm, and I'm choosing the diploma.'
Bade Papa grunted. Chachi smiled a little.

qa.q: Which form was Pradeep holding?
qa.a: The veterinary diploma form.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel on finding the verandah had already decided, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt pressured and a bit hurt, since his chest tightened, yet he also felt cared for, as he thanked them for thinking about him.

qa.q: What worked in Pradeep's reply to the family?
qa.a: He thanked them, asked about their worries and really listened, then calmly kept the final choice as his own.

qa.q: How might Chachi see Pradeep's decision after being listened to?
qa.a: Chachi may feel respected because the point about fees was heard, which could explain the small smile even though the choice went differently.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose course choice is discussed by relatives before he decides, feeling care and control together, and answering with thanks, listening and his own decision.

passage:
At the New Year table in his grandmother's house outside Osaka, Kaito had barely lifted his chopsticks when Uncle Hiro raised it. 'The bank in Kobe is hiring. I already spoke to someone.' Aunt Emi nodded; another uncle warned that small design studios close all the time. Kaito felt his face heat. The studio's offer, which his friend Daniel had first told him about, sat unanswered on his phone.
He bowed slightly. 'Thank you. I know you worry about my future, and that means a lot.' He asked Uncle Hiro what he liked about the bank, and listened.
That night he texted Daniel: 'Still taking the studio job. But I'll send Uncle a New Year card.'

qa.q: Where is the bank that is hiring?
qa.a: In Kobe.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when Uncle Hiro said he had already spoken to someone?
qa.a: Kaito felt embarrassed and a little cornered, his face heating, yet he also saw the worry behind it as care.

qa.q: Which of Kaito's choices at the table was wise, and why?
qa.a: Thanking the family and asking Uncle Hiro about the bank, because it kept the relationship warm while he still made his own choice.

qa.q: How might Uncle Hiro see Kaito taking the studio job?
qa.a: Uncle Hiro may feel disappointed or worried at first, but having been listened to may help him accept it more easily.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult whose job choice is taken up by uncles and aunts before he has decided, meeting it with thanks and listening while keeping the final say.

passage:
12 March
Tonight at dinner my son Rajat and his wife Vinita said they have found a two-room flat near her office. They said it softly, like people bringing bad news. I kept eating. Twenty-two years this house has held three generations; my own father built the back room for us. After they went up I sat on the terrace a long time. The house felt bigger and emptier already. But I also remember how tired Vinita looks after two hours on the bus. Tomorrow I will tell them: go, with my blessing. Only, Sunday lunch is here, and nobody comes out of duty. Come because you want to.
Pankaj

qa.q: Where is the flat that Rajat and Vinita found?
qa.a: Near Vinita's office.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling while sitting on the terrace?
qa.a: Pankaj felt sad and a sense of loss, as if the family house was already growing bigger and emptier.

qa.q: What was wise about Pankaj's plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: Blessing the move while asking for Sunday lunches out of love, not duty, keeps the family close in a new shape.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel when Pankaj gives the move a blessing?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and grateful, since the couple shared the news nervously, expecting it to hurt.

grounding: Shows an elder who feels the joint household slipping away as a grown son and his wife choose a smaller home, and who accepts the change while asking for regular, willing gatherings.

passage:
Rukmini: Sathya told us today. My son is moving out with his wife, to a flat across town.
Amandeep: Oh Rukmini. How are you feeling?

Rukmini: Maybe I will ask for festivals and one Sunday. Not force.
Amandeep: Yes. And tell Sathya you're proud.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling after hearing Sathya's news?
qa.a: Rukmini felt a deep loss, 'like the house lost its walls', and at the same time proud of Sathya.

qa.q: What approach did Amandeep suggest, and why might it work?

qa.q: How might Sathya feel if Rukmini asks only for festivals and one Sunday instead of objecting to the move?
qa.a: Sathya would likely feel relieved and free to visit gladly, since the move is accepted and the request is small and warm.

grounding: Illustrates an elder feeling the joint family slip away as a grown son moves to a smaller household, and choosing gentle regular gatherings over forced duty.

passage:
Thursday night
Signed nothing yet, but I saw the flat. One room, a window over a neem tree, twenty minutes from the office instead of ninety. Irfan, who found it, kept saying, 'Just tell them.' Easy for Irfan. At dinner Papa asked about my day and I talked about traffic, nothing else. Mummy's knee has been bad; who will take her to physio on Saturdays? If I leave, will the aunties say I abandoned them? I keep picturing announcing it all at once and Papa going silent. Maybe instead: sit with them on Sunday, tell them why, promise Saturdays and Sunday dinner, and actually mean it.
Ishita

qa.q: How far is the flat from the office?
qa.a: Twenty minutes from the office, instead of ninety.

qa.q: What is Ishita worried about when thinking of telling Mummy and Papa?
qa.a: Ishita feels guilty and afraid, worried about who will take Mummy to physio and that the aunties will call it abandoning the family.

qa.q: Which plan is better for Ishita, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with them on Sunday to explain and promising Saturdays and Sunday dinners, because an honest talk about visits and duties hurts less than a sudden announcement.

qa.q: How might Papa react if Ishita announced the move all at once?
qa.a: Papa might go silent and feel rejected or blindsided, which could turn a practical move into a wound.

grounding: Shows a young working adult who wants a separate flat but feels guilt about leaving the parents, and plans an honest talk about visits and duties instead of a sudden announcement.

passage:
